title: Fear and Opportunity in Moonlight: The Dynamic Effects of Lunar Illumination on the Behaviour of Terrestrial Vertebrate Species
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

Natural variation in lunar illumination changes the nocturnal visual environment and can alter animal behaviour, but responses may differ among taxa, traits, habitats, and behavioural contexts. We synthesized published evidence in the context of three non-mutually exclusive hypotheses concerning predation risk, visual performance, and foraging efficiency to assess whether terrestrial vertebrates respond consistently to brighter versus darker lunar conditions and whether these responses vary with taxonomic group, functional traits, habitat context, and phylogenetic relatedness.

Location

Global.

Time Period

1974–2024.

Major Taxa Studied

Mammals, birds, amphibians, and reptiles.

Methods

We conducted a meta-analysis integrating 231 studies with a total of 950 observations to assess the impact of moonlight on the behaviour of terrestrial vertebrates, including mammals, birds, amphibians, and reptiles. This study focused on linking behavioural responses to moonlight with species' life history and functional traits.

Results

Across all taxa, brighter lunar conditions were associated with a small positive mean effect on behavioural activity, but responses differed among vertebrate groups. Birds showed increased activity under brighter lunar conditions, mammals showed reduced activity, and amphibians and reptiles showed no significant overall response. Moderator analyses suggested that habitat openness, sensory mode, reproductive traits, and migration were associated with variation in mammal and bird responses. Mammals in open habitats and visually oriented mammals tended to show more positive responses, whereas mammals in dense habitats showed negative responses and increasing reproductive output was associated with more negative responses. In birds, open habitats and migratory behaviour were associated with more positive responses. Larger-bodied amphibians were more active on moonlit nights, consistent with a timing role of moonlight in synchronizing breeding and movements, with foraging efficiency contributing in some contexts. Although the overall effect in reptiles was not significant, responses varied with diel activity and habitat association.

Main Conclusions

Moonlight does not produce a single, uniform behavioural response across terrestrial vertebrates. Instead, responses to lunar illumination are taxon-specific and context dependent, reflecting differences in habitat structure, sensory ecology, movement ecology, and life-history traits. These results support a framework in which moonlight can either enhance behavioural opportunities or increase exposure risk depending on ecological context. Incorporating lunar illumination into trait-based and habitat-based studies of animal behaviour may improve predictions of how natural and artificial night-time light regimes influence terrestrial vertebrates.
